blocks.text: Robert Lopez
Director of Operations
Solis, Allen and Oconnell
Re: Stormwater Permit Support
Dear Mr. Lopez:

This letter follows our walk of the yard last month and sets down the terms on which we will help you obtain coverage under the stormwater permit your operation now requires and put the plan behind it into working order. I have written it so that the scope, the schedule, and the terms sit in one place and none of them is left to memory. If it reads the way we discussed, please sign the enclosed copy where indicated and return it to this office; the countersigned copy is the agreement between us. We will begin the work for {{fact:f:E-2021-001.client}} on {{fact:f:E-2021-001.start}}.
Scope of Services

The work has four parts, and each follows from the one before it. We will first characterize the site as it discharges, walking the property to find every point where stormwater leaves it, mapping the drainage areas that feed those points, and recording the materials and activities exposed to the rain along the way. On that basis we will prepare the Stormwater Pollution Prevention Plan the permit requires, written to your operation as it actually runs and not to a form. We will then file for coverage on your behalf, assembling and submitting the notice of intent and the materials the agency expects with it. And we will stand up the monitoring the permit will hold you to, taking the first round of samples ourselves so that the baseline in the file is one we collected and can stand behind. The design of new stormwater controls, and the construction of any of them, are not part of this engagement.
Approach

We do not write the plan from the office and check the site against it afterward. Someone walks the yard first, because what is exposed to stormwater is a matter of what is actually out there on a working day, and the yard is where that gets read. Where an outfall is hard to place, or a drainage area could be drawn two ways, we will say so and go back to look again before we commit to the tidy version. A plan that is honest about what it is still unsure of is one we can defend when a reviewer questions it later, and the sampling data behind it will be checked here before any of it is submitted.
Our Team

Two of our field technicians will do the site work. Heather Morton will run the sampling and the monitoring rounds; she holds a method steady from one visit to the next, which is the whole point of a baseline that has to stay comparable as the rounds go on. Joseph Nichols will handle the outfall survey and the field documentation, and he errs toward writing down more than less, which is what a record built to be checked wants. Among ourselves we use first names, but the names on anything that goes to the agency are the full ones, because that is the record that lasts. I read the plan and the sampling data myself before either leaves this office.
Schedule

We expect the work to run about four months from the start date above, allowing for the sampling to fall in usable weather and for the agency to take the time it takes once we have filed. The pace of the review after we submit is outside our hands, and we will not put a date on it. We will keep your office current as the work moves from the yard to the plan to the filing, so nothing about the schedule reaches you as a surprise.
Fees and Payment

Our fee for the work described above is {{fact:f:E-2021-001.fee}}, and it covers the site characterization, the plan, the permit filing, and the first round of monitoring. We invoice monthly for the work performed in the period and for the out-of-pocket costs the work requires, chiefly the laboratory analyses on the stormwater samples, and any agency fees are passed through at cost. Invoices are due within thirty days of the date they are rendered. If the site or the agency calls for something outside what is described here, we will tell you and agree the cost with you before we do the work.
Term and Termination

This agreement begins on {{fact:f:E-2021-001.start}} and continues until the plan is delivered, coverage is filed, and the first monitoring round is recorded, unless it is ended sooner. Either of us may end it on written notice to the other. If the work is stopped before it is finished, you will owe us for the work performed and the costs incurred through the date the notice takes effect, and nothing beyond that.
Confidentiality

We will keep what you share with us in confidence and use it only for this engagement, with one limit you should understand at the outset. A stormwater permit is filed in order to be granted, and once the plan and the supporting data go to the agency they become part of a public record. Beyond what the filing itself places on that record, we will not disclose your information without your consent, except where the law requires it of us.
Limitation of Liability

Our services will be performed with the care and skill ordinarily used by environmental professionals practicing in this area under similar conditions, and we make no other warranty, express or implied. The plan and the application are our professional work; whether coverage is granted, and on what conditions, rests with the agency, which has the final say. Our liability to you arising out of this engagement, from any cause, will not exceed the total fee payable under this agreement, and neither of us will be liable to the other for consequential or indirect damages.
Governing Law

This agreement is governed by the laws of the state in which the site is located. It states the whole of our understanding on this work, replaces the discussions and correspondence that came before it, and may be changed only by a writing that both of us sign.

If this letter states our agreement correctly, please sign both copies where shown, keep one for your file, and return the other to this office. Once the signed copy is in hand we will call to set the first site visit. We are glad to be taking this on with Solis, Allen and Oconnell, and we will give the yard and the numbers the same care we give the reports that follow from them.
Very truly yours,
To: Project Team
From: Heather Morton
Re: Stormwater Permit Support for Solis, Allen and Oconnell

The signed scope is back, so the stormwater permit support for Solis, Allen and Oconnell is underway. What we owe {{fact:f:E-2021-001.client}} is easy to state and careful to do: a Stormwater Pollution Prevention Plan that fits how their yard actually runs, a permit filing the agency will accept without a second request, and a first round of monitoring that leaves a baseline we can stand behind years from now. I have written this memo so the work divides cleanly and each piece has an owner before anyone drives out to the site. Read it against your own part and tell me if I have a boundary wrong.

One word on how we keep the record, because the plan will only ever be as good as what we write on the walk. We record as we go, at the outfall and in the yard, and not from memory once we are back at the desk. Where something is ambiguous, note the ambiguity and mark it for a second look instead of resolving it in your head, since the baseline the later rounds are read against has to be clean.
How the work divides

items: Site characterization. Walk the property and find every point where stormwater leaves it, then map the drainage area that feeds each one and note the materials and activities exposed to the rain along the way. Joseph Nichols leads the outfall survey and the field documentation behind it.

Stormwater plan. Draft the pollution prevention plan to the site as we find it on the walk rather than to a form, and tie each control back to the activity it is meant to address, so a reviewer can follow why it is there.

Monitoring. Stand up the sampling program and take the first round ourselves, so the baseline in the file is one we collected. I will run the sampling and hold the method steady from point to point, which is what makes the rounds that follow comparable to it.
Permit filing. Assemble the notice of intent and the supporting materials, and file for coverage once the plan is drafted and the baseline is recorded, in that order and not before.

blocks.text: Everything that goes to the agency is checked here before it leaves. The plan is read and the sampling data is reconciled in the office ahead of any submission, so build that review into your part instead of treating the filing as the day the work ends. A total none of us has checked is not one the firm will file.

The order among these matters. The plan and the monitoring both rest on the site walk, so nothing downstream is firm until the outfalls are placed and the drainage areas are drawn. We will keep the plan in draft until the walk is finished and not commit to a layout we might have to redraw once we are standing in the yard.

Robert Lopez is our contact at Solis, Allen and Oconnell, and anything that needs site access or a decision from their side runs through him. The engagement dates from {{fact:f:E-2021-001.start}} and runs about four months, which puts us at the very front of it, with the field work first and the filing last. I will confirm access with him before we set any field day, and keep his office posted as we move from the walk to the plan to the filing, so nothing on the schedule reaches the client as a surprise.
First step

The one thing to do this week is the site walk. Send me your availability for the first field day by Friday, and I will set the day with Robert Lopez around the weather. Once we have walked the yard together, I will send the sampling schedule and the point list.

blocks.text: Discussion

The work is on schedule at this point in the engagement, and nothing found so far changes the scope agreed at the start. The site has been walked, the outfalls are placed, and the pollution prevention plan is in draft. What stands between here and the filing is the plan's completion and the first monitoring round.

Heather Morton and I walked the property and identified the points where stormwater leaves the site. Two of them are straightforward. A third, at the back of the yard where two drainage areas appear to meet, can be read as one outfall or as two, and it has been recorded both ways pending a return visit, so the plan does not commit to a boundary we are not yet sure of.

The outfall survey was documented in full. Each point carries a photograph and a sketch keyed to the drainage map, so the placement can be checked without a second trip by anyone who was not there. Where a drainage boundary was inferred rather than seen on the ground, it is marked as inferred on the map.

The plan is drafted to the site as it was found on the walk, and each control in it is tied to the activity it is meant to address, so a reviewer can see why it is there. The single open item is the back outfall, which the draft flags rather than resolves.

The first monitoring round for {{fact:f:E-2021-001.client}} was discussed. The sampling points follow the confirmed outfalls, and the round will be scheduled once the back outfall is settled, so the baseline is not taken against a point that may still move. The results will be checked in the office before they are entered as the baseline.

The sampling plan itself was reviewed. One sample will be taken at each confirmed outfall during a qualifying rain, with the field record completed at the point and the chain of custody kept from the yard to the laboratory. The round is a baseline, so the method is set now and held for the rounds that follow, which is what lets a later reviewer read them against each other.

Mr. Lopez confirmed that access will stay open for the field team through the sampling. He also noted a change in the yard's material storage since the walk, which will be carried into the plan before it is finalized, since the plan is meant to match the yard as it actually runs.

The immediate next step is the return visit to the back outfall. Once it is settled as one point or two, the monitoring round can be scheduled and the plan finalized against it, and the filing follows both. It was agreed that nothing is filed until the outfall is resolved and the first round is recorded.
Action Items

rows: Return to the back outfall and settle whether it is one point or two
Finalize the pollution prevention plan against the confirmed outfalls
Carry the change in material storage into the plan
Keep site access open through the sampling round

blocks.text: Status Report: Stormwater Permit Support
Prepared for Solis, Allen and Oconnell
Prepared by Heather Morton, Field Technician, Saltmarsh Environmental Partners
Where things stand

We are about halfway through the stormwater permit support for {{fact:f:E-2021-001.client}}, and the work is running the way we planned it. The field characterization of the site is essentially done, the pollution prevention plan is in draft, and we are moving toward the first round of monitoring and the permit filing. Nothing to this point has fallen outside the scope we agreed at the start.

The picture is close to what we expected. The yard drains about the way the site suggested it would, with one point at the back of the property that we are looking at again before we commit the plan to it. We recorded what we found as we went, so the plan and the filing will rest on the field record and not on anyone's memory of the day.

For where we are in the engagement, the balance of the work now shifts from the field to the desk and the filing. The heavy field days are largely behind us; what is left is one return visit, the baseline round, and the paperwork that turns the plan into an application. That is the stretch where our checking matters most, so we have built the review time into the schedule and are not treating the filing date as the day the work ends.
What we completed this period

items: Joseph Nichols and I walked the property, identified the points where stormwater leaves the site, and mapped the drainage area feeding each one.
We documented each outfall with a photograph and a sketch keyed to the drainage map, so the placement can be checked without a return trip.
We drafted the Stormwater Pollution Prevention Plan to the site as we found it, tying each control to the activity it addresses.
We flagged one outfall at the back of the yard, where two drainage areas appear to meet, for a return visit instead of committing to a boundary we were unsure of.
We set the monitoring point list against the confirmed outfalls, so the baseline round is taken against points that will not move.

blocks.text: The one item worth drawing out of that list is the back outfall. The two drainage areas there could be read as meeting at one point or at two, and because the reading changes where a sample would be taken, we are resolving it with a return visit before the baseline round. Leaving it unsettled would put a question into the file at the exact point a reviewer looks first.

A note on the data, since it is what the baseline will stand on. Every outfall carries a completed field record, a photograph, and a sketch tied to the drainage map, and each is entered and checked in the office before it becomes part of the file. When the first round comes back from the laboratory, the results are reconciled against the field record before any of it is read as the baseline, because a baseline the firm cannot trace is one it cannot defend later.
What comes next

items: Return to the back outfall and settle whether it is one point or two.
Take the first monitoring round against the confirmed points, and check the results in the office before they are entered as the baseline.
Finalize the pollution prevention plan against the confirmed outfalls and the yard as it now runs.
File the notice of intent and the supporting materials for permit coverage once the plan and the baseline are in hand.

blocks.text: On the budget, the work remains within the {{fact:f:E-2021-001.fee}} fee agreed for the engagement, and we do not see anything at this point that would carry it past that figure. The costs still ahead are chiefly the laboratory analyses on the first sampling round, which sit within what we allowed. Should the site or the agency ask for something outside the scope, we will tell you and agree the cost with you before we do the work.
Risks and watch items

A few things are worth naming now, and none of them is blocking. The back outfall could move a sampling point slightly when we resolve it, though we do not expect it to shift the plan. The sampling depends on usable weather, so a round could slip a few days. And once we file, the agency's review runs on its own clock, which is outside our hands and yours.

We raise these now because they are the kind of thing you would want to know early. None of them changes the scope or what we expect the outcome to be; they are the usual friction of getting a permit filed, and we are tracking them so you do not have to.
Next step

The next thing you will see from us is confirmation that the back outfall is settled and the first monitoring round is scheduled. We will call your office once the return visit is done, and from there the plan and the filing follow in short order.
